![](../../src/images/hex_complex.png){.intro_image}

The fundamental data object in R is the **atomic vector**. Atomic vectors form the building block of every other data object that we will use in this course, and in fact any *single* value in R (a single number, a single word) is itself an atomic vector. An atomic vector can be described by its **class**, which tells us what kind of values it contains. All values within a single atomic vector must share the same class.

In this lesson, we will explore the four classes of atomic vectors that you will encounter most often in this course. You will learn:

* The difference between double numeric and integer vectors
* How to work with character values, including when single quotes are (and are not) necessary
* What a factor is and why the order of its levels matters
* How logical values are stored and tested, including a common mistake that catches almost everyone at least once

[{{< fa exclamation-triangle size=2x >}} Important!]{style="color: red;"} This lesson assumes that you have completed [Preliminary Lesson 2: Environment & Functions](0.2_environment_and_functions.qmd){target="_blank"}. As the material covered herein will build on the content in that lesson, please do not proceed until its completion.

</div>

## Before you begin

To get the most out of this lesson, please:

* Open RStudio in a clean session;
* Open a new, blank script file and save it as "lesson_0.3.R";
* Code along with the content!

## Numbers

There are two kinds of number values that we will work with in this course:

* **Double numeric**: For our purposes, this can be thought of as a decimal number
* **Integer**: A whole number

Let's create an atomic vector of numbers and assign it to the name `number_object`:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true

number_object <-
  c(1, 1, 2, 3)

number_object
```

We can determine the class of the vector with the `class` function:

```{webr}
class(number_object)
```

How an atomic vector is stored in your computer is known as its **type**. We use `typeof` to determine this:

```{webr}
typeof(number_object)
```

Notice that numbers created with `c()` are stored as double numeric by default -- even though every value we supplied was a whole number!

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [True or false: Numeric values created with `c()`, such as `c(1, 1, 2, 3)`, are stored as integer type by default because they are whole numbers.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r torf(FALSE)`
:::

To generate an integer vector of adjacent whole numbers, we use the colon function (`:`), which generates a regular sequence from a starting to an ending value:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true

my_integers <- 1:3

class(my_integers)

typeof(my_integers)
```

If we want to generate an integer vector with `c()`, we add an uppercase `L` after each value:

```{webr}
class(
  c(1L, 1L, 2L, 3L)
)
```

We can also convert a double numeric vector to an integer vector with `as.integer`:

```{webr}
class(
  as.integer(
    c(1, 1, 2, 3)
  )
)
```

::: mysecret
{{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [`as.integer()` truncates, it does not round!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`as.integer()` is only safe to use if the values that you are converting are already whole numbers. Notice what happens when we convert decimal values to integers:

```{r}
as.integer(
  c(1.1, 2.3, 5.8)
)
```

`as.integer()` truncated (i.e., dropped) the decimal portion of each value rather than rounding to the nearest whole number.
:::

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [True or false: `as.integer(c(1.1, 2.3, 5.8))` rounds each value to the nearest whole number.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r torf(FALSE)`
:::

Likewise, we use `as.numeric` to convert an integer vector to a double numeric vector:

```{webr}
class(
  as.numeric(1:3)
)

typeof(
  as.numeric(1:3)
)
```

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Test your knowledge!]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

1. Which of the following produces an atomic vector whose type is integer?

`r longmcq(c("c(1, 2, 3)", answer = "1:3", "c(1.0, 2.0, 3.0)", "as.numeric(1:3)"))`

## Characters

A **character** value is a symbol or set of symbols from a given alphabet (this may also include numbers and punctuation). When a character value is made up of more than one symbol, it is often called a **string**.

Character values are always enclosed in quotation marks. The code below creates a character vector and assigns it to the name `months`:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true

months <-
  c(
    "March",
    "February",
    "January",
    "January"
  )
```

The class and type of a character vector are both `"character"`:

```{webr}
class(months)

typeof(months)
```

Any atomic vector can be converted to a character vector with `as.character`:

```{webr}
as.character(1:5)
```

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Which function converts an atomic vector of any class into a character vector?]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r longmcq(c(answer = "as.character()", "as.numeric()", "typeof()", "c()"))`
:::

### Single or double quotes?

Single (`'hello world'`) and double (`"hello world"`) quotes can largely be used interchangeably in R. **In this course, we will always use double quotes for character values** -- this is the convention set out in our [style guide](../module_1/1.6_course_style_guide.qmd){target="_blank"} and it matches the [tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#character-vectors){target="_blank"}.

There is exactly one situation in which you will need to reach for single quotes: when the character value itself contains a double quote. Watch what happens when we try to enclose a quoted phrase in double quotes:

```{r}
#| error: true

"Maude said, "to me they will always be glorious birds""
```

R reads the second double quote as the *end* of the string, and has no idea what to do with the text that follows. We can resolve this by enclosing the entire value in single quotes instead:

```{r}
'Maude said, "to me they will always be glorious birds"'
```

The reverse problem occurs if a character value contains an apostrophe and is enclosed in single quotes:

```{r}
#| error: true

'Maude's Cadillac'
```

Because our course convention is to default to double quotes, this particular problem should rarely come up -- but it is worth knowing that the fix is the same in either direction (switch to the other kind of quote) or that you can **escape** the problematic character with a backslash, which tells R to treat the following character literally:

```{r}
"Maude's Cadillac"

'Maude said, "to me they will always be glorious birds"'

"Maude said, \"to me they will always be glorious birds\""
```

::: mysecret
{{< fa screwdriver-wrench size=2x >}} [So when *should* I use single quotes?]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

Only when the character value contains a double quote. If you find yourself reaching for single quotes for any other reason, switch back to double quotes -- this is one of the rules that our automated style checks will flag!
:::

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Test your knowledge!]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

1. You need a character value that itself contains a double quote. Which approach works?

`r longmcq(c(answer = "Enclose the whole value in single quotes, or escape the inner double quote with a backslash", "There is no way to include a double quote in a string", "Type two double quotes in a row", "Remove the inner quote -- R does not allow it"))`

2. True or false: in this course, single and double quotes should be used interchangeably, based on whichever you happen to type first.

`r torf(FALSE)`
:::

## Factors

A **factor** is a value that maps character labels onto integers. A factor contains three pieces of information:

* **Integer values**: An integer associated with each factor level.
* **Levels**: The character values associated with each integer.
* **Labels**: The character values used when the factor is printed or plotted (these may differ from the levels).

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [A factor stores three pieces of information. Which set correctly names them?]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r longmcq(c("Class, type, and dimension", answer = "Integer values, levels, and labels", "Names, values, and attributes", "Rows, columns, and cells"))`
:::

Factors are useful when a character value can be grouped into one of a few categories (e.g., "juvenile" and "adult"), especially when you care about the order those categories are displayed in (e.g., "small", "medium", "large").

We create a factor with the `factor` function, supplying a character vector as the first argument:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true

example_factor <-
  factor(
    c(
      "one",
      "one",
      "two",
      "three"
    )
  )

class(example_factor)

typeof(example_factor)
```

Notice that the type is `"integer"` even though we typed in words!

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [True or false: A factor is stored in your computer as an integer type, even though you create it by supplying a character vector to `factor()`.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r torf(TRUE)`
:::

Let's have a look at the object itself:

```{webr}
example_factor
```

There are four values, but they have been grouped into three levels. We can see the integers mapped to each level with `as.integer`:

```{webr}
as.integer(example_factor)
```

::: mysecret
{{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [Factor levels are ordered alphabetically by default!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

Notice that "one" was assigned the integer 1, "three" was assigned 2, and "two" was assigned 3 -- that's alphabetical order, not the order in which the values appeared! This can cause real problems when a factor's levels have a natural, non-alphabetical order (e.g., "low", "medium", "high").
:::

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [True or false: When you create a factor with `factor()` without specifying levels, the levels are ordered according to the order in which the values first appear in the data.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r torf(FALSE)`
:::

We can plot a factor to see the count of values at each level:

```{webr}
plot(example_factor)
```

Given the x-axis labels, this order doesn't make a lot of sense. We can manually set the level order with the `levels` argument:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true

plot(
  factor(
    c("one", "one", "two", "three"),
    levels = c("one", "two", "three")
  )
)
```

## Logical values

R reserves the words `TRUE` and `FALSE` as **logical constants**. These are mapped to the integers 0 (`FALSE`) and 1 (`TRUE`), which means we can evaluate them numerically:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true

FALSE + TRUE

mean(
  c(FALSE, TRUE)
)
```

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [True or false: The logical constants `TRUE` and `FALSE` are mapped to the integers 1 and 0, so `FALSE + TRUE` evaluates to 1.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r torf(TRUE)`
:::

### Logical operators

We generate logical values by testing an object with a **logical operator**:

| Operator | Usage      | Meaning                                    |
|:--------:|:----------:|:-------------------------------------------|
| `==`     | `x == y`   | x is equal to y                            |
| `!=`     | `x != y`   | x is NOT equal to y                        |
| `!`      | `!(x)`     | NOT x                                      |
| `\|`     | `x \| y`   | x OR y                                     |
| `&`      | `x & y`    | x AND y                                    |
| `%in%`   | `x %in% y` | x is a set of values found within y        |
| `<`      | `x < y`    | x is less than y                           |
| `<=`     | `x <= y`   | x is less than or equal to y               |
| `>`      | `x > y`    | x is greater than y                        |
| `>=`     | `x >= y`   | x is greater than or equal to y            |

```{webr}
3 < 4

3 > 4

2:4 == 3
```

::: mysecret
{{< fa screwdriver-wrench size=2x >}} [Be careful when comparing two sets of values with `==`!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

This is one of the most common mistakes that early R users make (we will see it again, applied to data frames, in ***Lesson 1.3: R Objects***). Notice what happens when we compare two integer vectors of the same length with `==`:

```{r}
2:4 == 1:3
```

You might expect two of these to evaluate to `TRUE` -- but `==` compares values *by position*, not by set membership. To test whether values in one vector are found *anywhere* in another, use `%in%` instead:

```{r}
2:4 %in% 1:3
```
:::

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [True or false: Comparing two equal-length vectors with `==` tests set membership, so `2:4 == 1:3` returns `TRUE` wherever a value on the left also appears anywhere on the right.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r torf(FALSE)`
:::

:::

<button class="accordion" style="margin-bottom: 1em;">Solution</button>
::: panel

```{r}
summer %in% spring

```
:::

## Take-home points

Before you move on, here are the ideas from this lesson that are most worth holding onto:

* The **atomic vector** is R's fundamental object -- even a single number or word is one -- and every value in a given vector shares the same **class** (what it holds) and **type** (how it's stored).
* With numbers, `c()` gives you **double** by default even when every value is a whole number; use `:` or an `L` suffix (like `1L`) when you actually want **integer**.
* Reach for `as.integer()` only on values that are already whole, because it **truncates** the decimal portion rather than rounding -- so `as.integer(2.8)` gives you 2, not 3.
* For characters, default to **double quotes** in this course; single quotes are only needed when the value itself contains a double quote (or you can **escape** that quote with a backslash), and `as.character()` will coerce any vector to character.
* A **factor** maps character labels onto integers, which is why its `typeof()` is integer; unless you say otherwise, its levels are ordered **alphabetically**, not in the order the values appeared.
* Take control of a factor with the `levels` argument to set the order and the `labels` argument to rename the categories -- and remember `labels` are matched in the order of the `levels`, so setting labels without levels can mislabel a category.
* Logical `TRUE`/`FALSE` are stored as 1 and 0, so you can `sum()` them to count `TRUE`s or take their `mean()` to get a proportion.
* Finally, `==` compares **by position** while `%in%` tests **set membership** -- so when you want to know whether values appear *anywhere* in another vector, reach for `%in%`, not `==`.
